A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CROW study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive restructuring.

before.justification: v1 reports original backdoor-mitigation results, helpfulness evaluations, ablations and jailbreak experiments in Tables 1–8.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original baseline comparisons, component ablations, semantic-backdoor results and training-loss plots.

M1.justification: CROW retains FGSM perturbations of input embeddings and finetuning with language-modeling loss plus weighted, perturbed layer-consistency loss. The algorithms are consolidated. Pure Consistency and embedding-only consistency are added as experimental ablations, without changing the proposed CROW procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds SST-2 alongside Alpaca and two semantic/entity-trigger scenarios targeting negative sentiment about Joe Biden. This is a focused extension of data and trigger coverage; the original sentiment-steering, refusal, code-injection and jailbreak evaluations remain.

E2.justification: v1 explicitly excludes CleanGen from evaluation, whereas v2 Table 9 compares it with CROW across five attacks and two Llama-2-7B tasks. This adds a directly relevant LLM defense beyond the retained finetuning, pruning and quantization baselines. Tables 10–11 also introduce comparisons with two component-removal variants.

E3.justification: The added semantic experiments specify 1% poisoning, three epochs, batch size 128 and learning rate 2e-5; Appendices C.2–C.3 introduce controlled component-removal comparisons. The original main evaluation settings and metrics are retained. Newly specifying five-epoch LoRA training for CROW does not establish a change to the earlier experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained perturbation-magnitude, weighting-factor and similarity-measure studies, v2 tests removing adversarial perturbations (Table 10) and restricting consistency to embeddings (Table 11). It also adds semantic-trigger robustness experiments and training-stability curves. These directly examine previously untested design choices and robustness questions.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, reports uncertainty intervals or error bars, or provides significance tests. The added tables and training curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 retain their numerical values, but Tables 9–12 and Figure 3 add substantial results. Pure Consistency leaves 48.97% BadNets refusal ASR versus CROW's 19.63%; the new semantic-instruction experiment reports 89.10% without defense versus 3.52% with CROW. Table 9 also reveals tradeoffs: CleanGen has higher MT-Bench scores throughout, while CROW has lower ASR on four of five refusal attacks.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds a bounded-hidden-state-norm assumption and an order-(tau/c)^2 argument connecting cosine consistency to Euclidean distances. It also changes the final perturbation comparison from a strict non-amplification inequality in v1 Equation 14 to approximate equality in v2 Equation 10. The underlying Jacobian/Lipschitz argument remains.

C1.justification: The central claims about reference-free, trigger-agnostic defense, limited clean data, preserved utility and computational efficiency remain. The introduction drops v1's explicit claim to the most comprehensive evaluation, retaining the contribution of evaluation across six attacks, five models and three tasks.

C2.justification: New appendix discussion interprets the ablations as explaining why adversarial perturbations and consistency across layers are needed, and expands CleanGen deployment tradeoffs. Section 3.3 clarifies that stable behavior refers to the regularized model. The existing hyperparameter-tuning and adaptive-attack limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies five-epoch LoRA finetuning for CROW, clarifies elementwise embedding perturbations, and documents semantic-experiment hyperparameters. Conversely, v1's 200-sample Figure 1 diagnostic count and 32 GB RAM detail are omitted. The code repository disclosure is retained.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning against closely related mechanisms, including trigger-activated change and channel Lipschitzness, layer-wise feature analysis, EP-BNP, adversarial-training defenses and W2SDefense. CleanGen changes from an excluded comparator to an evaluated complementary approach. These revisions materially sharpen CROW's relationship to prior defenses.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology and results discussion are extensively condensed and rewritten. Background and experimental details move into Appendices A–B, method subsections are merged, the separate Key Observations section is removed, and ethical considerations move into an Impact Statement.

P2.justification: The conference layout substantially reflows and restyles the document and tables, consolidates two algorithm displays into one, and adds Figure 3 and Tables 9–12. Figures 1–2 retain identical images. The original attack-example Table 9 is retained as Table 13 with revised formatting.

improvement.justification: The CleanGen comparison and component ablations address important gaps in v1: no evaluated LLM-specific defense and no direct tests isolating CROW's defining components. Together with semantic-trigger experiments and closer prior-work positioning, they substantially strengthen the empirical justification. Some new experimental settings remain unspecified and uncertainty reporting is still absent. Rewritten prose also incorrectly describes the 91.50% to 85.28% ASR change as an increase, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger validation.
